title: What old game made an art direction choice that no studio would dare make today?
author: Square_Reason_6490
selftext:
I’m thinking less about technical limitations and more about genuinely weird, bold, or risky visual decisions. Character designs, color palettes, UI, environments, animation, anything.  
What game made a visual choice that would probably get killed in a modern art review, but somehow worked?

I’m just hoping to learn and get inspired by your suggestions

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: Okami went for a stylized look that seemed impossible at the time. Now it still doesn't look dated for a PS2 game.

replies.author: Square_Reason_6490
replies.body: Yeah that’s a pretty popular one for its look, I was hoping for some deep cuts that were overlooked by most

comments.author: pixelvspixel
comments.body: The Neverhood was a really standout game at the time, that took some pretty big art production risk.

comments.author: Decent_Assist_4811
comments.body: Vib Ribbon reduced visuals to the max so it could preload audio and create levels from it.

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: Iirc you could even replace the disc and play levels based on your music

comments.author: Upper-Philosophy2376
comments.body:
Vagrant Story still has a unique look, a low poly with lots of texture and sort of comic inspired. I see a lot of artists making things that are low poly with pixel textures though I can't think of a game that has released with that style, but I think it has a lot of potential.   
Comix Zone for SNES had you jumping through comic book panels.   
Donkey Kong Country and Killer Instinct on SNES's art style would probably be rejected in a modern art review, they took 3D models and made pixel compressed images of them then animated them as if pixel art, at the time it gave what felt like a high tech look, now it would look like low effort.   
Ghost Trick for NDS has a really good anime with lineart style for Character Art.  
Guardian Heroes for Sega Saturn has a unique style, it's sort of pixel art but sort of low poly, but also unqiue anime style.   
In fact a lot of pixel art games for the Saturn were pretty good visually, Astal, Princess Crown, KEIO 2, and more.  
Metal Slug is still the king of Pixel Art though, and early Street Fighter games are still the king of animating characters. I've also always really liked the Scott Pilgrim games pixel art if you want a more cute/chibi style.   
Breath of Fire 3 might also be a kind of peak pixel art, though it doesn't have lineart so it has a more painterly feel.   
if you want to go super minimal though N+ should give some inspiration.   
For exagerated toon proportions one of my favorites is Disney's Guilty Party for Wii.   
XIII and Killer 7 on gamecube, both had incredible cell shading. 

As for interesting UX the DS/3DS obscure puzzle games like Sudoku/Picross/Dictionaries that were never released in english have really interesting UI/UX direction. I think your best UX inspiration will come from this era of handhelds, DS/3DS/PSP, and often from more obscure/strange games. Also even though a lot of people didn't like Pokemon Sword/Shield for gameplay reasons it also has some of the best UI in it's series.
